extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and applicants (AMS / patent professionals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing patentability, unity, and clarity of inventions in patent applications (claims, description, drawings) including exclusions (medical methods, biological processes), computer-implemented inventions, and procedures for unity objections and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-step test for excluded subject matter / technical character
rubrics_metrics.description: One approach consists in applying the following four steps: 1. Properly construe the claim; 2. Identify the actual contribution made by the invention; 3. Determine whether the actual contribution falls solely within the excluded subject matter or not 'as such'; and 4. Determine whether the actual or alleged contribution is actually technical in nature ('Technical contribution').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it passes the test for having technical character, the examiner then proceeds to the examination of other substantive aspects, such as novelty and inventive step. The examiner must objectively investigate the contribution actually made and is not bound to accept the contribution claimed by the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'computer-implemented invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Computer-implemented invention' is a term primarily intended to cover claims involving computers, computer networks or other programmable apparatus wherein at least one feature is implemented by means of a computer program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A computer program (sequence of executable instructions) and a corresponding computer-implemented method (method performed on a computer) are distinct. Claims directed to a computer-implemented method cannot be objected to as non-patentable subject matter because any method involving technical means (e.g. a computer) and technical means themselves (e.g. a computer or computer-readable storage medium) have technical character and thus represent inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: methods for treatment of the human or animal body
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent laws exclude methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery, therapy or diagnosis from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to ensure medical/veterinary practitioners are not hindered by patent rights. Therapeutic instruments/apparatus and products (substances/compositions) for use in therapeutic methods are not excluded. A method claim with even one step defining a therapeutic activity would fall under this prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for 'method of therapy' exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as the treatment cures, prevents or alleviates a disease, the treatment constitutes a method of therapy whether performed by practitioner, patient, or an automated system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-therapeutic treatments (e.g., chemical contraception, cosmetic treatments) may be patentable. Example: purely cosmetic treatment by chemical product considered patentable; cosmetic treatment involving surgery or therapy is not. A step of administering a substance for prophylactic reasons in a method claim would likely render the claim unpatentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for 'method of diagnosis' exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of diagnosis must include the deductive step which leads to a diagnosis and a recommended treatment; diagnostic methods are excluded only if performed on the living human or animal body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An extra-corporeal method (e.g., tests on removed blood samples) may be patentable. A treatment or diagnostic method performed on a deceased body is not excluded. Diagnostic methods are excluded only if limited to being carried out on the living body. The claim must include steps covering: (i) examination/data collection, (ii) comparison with standard values, (iii) finding significant deviation (a symptom), (iv) attribution of deviation to a clinical picture (deductive decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment/diagnosis on removed tissues or fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of body tissues or fluids after removal from the body, or diagnostic methods applied thereon, are not excluded from patentability insofar as these tissues/fluids are not returned to the same body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: diagnostic testing of stored blood in a blood bank is not excluded, whereas a dialysis treatment returning blood to the same body could be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plants, animals and 'essentially biological processes' exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant and animal varieties are excluded from patentability in AMS, but transgenic plants and genetically modified animals (except in some jurisdictions) and methods of making them may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a process is 'essentially biological' depends on degree of technical intervention by man; significant technical intervention that determines/controls the result means the process is not excluded. Product claims for plant/animal varieties cannot be allowed even if produced by microbiological process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturally occurring micro-organisms and microbiological processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Micro-organisms exist as part of Nature and may be treated as discoveries (not patentable) in some AMS, but most AMS don't exclude microorganisms from patentability; PCT: microbiological processes and the products thereof are not excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'microbiological process' covers processes using microorganisms and processes for producing microorganisms (e.g., genetic engineering). 'Product of a microbiological process' covers plasmids and viruses. Plant cells/tissues able to regenerate a full plant may be excluded from patentability if the originating plant was produced exclusively by an essentially biological process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmaceutical products, drugs & foodstuffs patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharmaceutical products, drugs and foodstuffs are not excluded from patentability in AMS except in Least Developed Countries (LDCs) where flexibility exists under WTO/TRIPS decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note regarding LDCs: key TRIPS provisions do not apply to pharmaceutical products in LDCs until at least January 2033 (possible extension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Unity of Invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application can claim only one invention or a group of closely related inventions. Unity requires that claims relate to a single invention, or to a group of inventions linked by a single general inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A group shares a 'single general inventive concept' if the inventions, as defined by the claims and interpreted in light of the description and drawings, have the same or corresponding special technical features that achieve the same technical effect or solve the same technical problem. Unity is relevant only to pre-grant proceedings and lack of unity is not a ground for revocation after grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria for unity of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner assesses unity by determining whether two or more inventions in the claims have the same or corresponding special technical features determined from the claims, description, drawings and common general knowledge as of the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Same' or 'corresponding' means special technical features achieve the same technical effect or solve the same technical problem; correspondence may be in alternative solutions or interrelated features (e.g., interaction between plug and socket). If inventions share such a feature they fulfill unity requirements; examples provided (spring vs rubber block both achieving resilience).

rubrics_metrics.name: No lack of unity between independent claim and its dependent claims/juxtaposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of unity does not arise if one claim contains a number of individual features which merely present a juxtaposition and do not present a technical interrelationship; by definition no lack of unity exists between an independent claim and its dependent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objection for lack of unity should not be raised on narrow, literal or academic grounds; there should be a broad, practical consideration of interdependence in relation to the state of the art, and benefit of doubt afforded to the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum reasoning methodology for lack of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess non-unitary subject matter, the patent office may apply 'minimum reasoning' methodology: identify common or corresponding subject-matter (if any); explain why this subject-matter cannot provide a single general inventive concept due to lack of same/corresponding special technical features; explain why there is no technical relationship among the inventions, if not apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis may include indicating non-common technical features and why claims may be grouped, statement why these features are different, identification of technical properties for each group and explanation why technical properties are different. Examples in PCT ISPE GL paragraphs referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors and examples in minimum reasoning (field-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on the technical field, identification of technical properties may show that members of a grouping of alternatives are not of a similar nature, intermediate/final products lack same essential structural element, a process is not specially adapted to production of a product, or a product/use does not provide a single general inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent office should not raise lack of unity merely because inventions are classified in separate classification groups or to restrict search to certain groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori vs a posteriori assessment of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of unity may be assessed 'a priori' (before considering prior art) or 'a posteriori' (after considering prior art); majority of AMS use both approaches; some jurisdictions (e.g., Lao PDR) assess a priori only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners usually form a prima facie unity opinion before search, then reconsider during/after search and at substantive examination; findings may be superseded by new facts/evidence. Whether a technical feature makes a 'contribution' over prior art (and thus constitutes a 'special technical feature') is considered with respect to novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of unity with regard to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner determines 'special technical features' from the claims in light of description, drawings and common general knowledge. If prior art shows that a claimed linking feature lacks novelty or is obvious, the linking feature may be denied 'special technical feature' status a posteriori and lack of unity may arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two or more groups have the same (corresponding) special technical feature they make the same contribution over prior art and unity is present. Example: polymeric compound A and a container composed of A both share polymeric compound A as special technical feature and thus unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions and remedies when lack of unity is found (appeal/options)
rubrics_metrics.description: If examiner determines application lacks unity, they inform applicant and describe inventions not deemed subject of examination and reasons; claimed subject-matter is divided into separate inventions/groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant should be given five options: appeal against examiner's decision or file counter statement at patent office; amend the claims; delete the claims said to be directed to other invention(s); file divisional application(s); abandon/withdraw the application. Appeal rights and procedures vary by AMS; in some countries certain rejections cannot be appealed but counter-arguments may be submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: clarity and conciseness of abstract, claims, description, drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: All AMS require the abstract, claims, description, and drawings, if any, of a patent application to be clear and concise. If unclear such that no meaningful opinion can be formed on novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability, examination may be restricted to claims/parts sufficiently clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an opinion cannot be established on a claim the examiner may issue an objection for lack of clarity. Issues of clarity should be raised separately from novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability. The clarity of claims is of utmost importance in formulating an opinion on novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT claim requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT Guidelines require that the claims must: (i) 'define the matter for which protection is sought'; (ii) 'be clear and concise'; and (iii) 'be fully supported by the description.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirement that claims be clear applies to individual claims and to the claims as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and content of claims (technical features; two-part form; reliance on description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be drafted in terms of the 'technical features of the invention.' The two-part form should be used 'whenever appropriate.' The claims must not, with respect to technical features, rely on references to the description or drawings 'except where absolutely necessary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims and description may contain chemical or mathematical formulae but not drawings. Any claim may contain tables 'if the subject matter of the claim makes the use of tables desirable' — examiners should not object to convenient use of tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of claims; independent and dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Two basic kinds of claim: claims to a physical entity (product, apparatus) and claims to an activity (process, use). All applications will contain one or more independent main claims directed to essential features of the invention. Dependent claims concern specific forms and must include essential features of at least one independent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT ISPE GL sections apply mutatis mutandis; see other sections for product-by-process, means-plus-function, product/apparatus limitations in process claims, and inconsistencies between claims and description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of claims (PSIA standard and transition phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be read giving words the ordinary meaning and scope as attributed by a person skilled in the relevant art (PSIA), unless description explicitly gives special meaning. A claim to a substance/composition for a particular use should be construed as meaning a substance/composition suitable for the stated use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating novelty/inventive step, examiner should consider transition phrase used ('consisting of', 'comprising', 'characterized by', 'consisting essentially of') as it affects subject-matter to be searched. Means-plus-function claims, product-by-process claims, and product/apparatus limitations in process claims have specific guidance (PCT ISPE GL references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for claim clarity (PSIA can determine boundaries; breadth vs clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of terms of a claim must be clear for a PSIA from the claim wording alone. Clarity must be analysed in light of application disclosure, teachings of prior art, and PSIA interpretation at time of invention. If PSIA can determine boundaries with reasonable degree of certainty, claim complies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breadth is not equivalent to lack of clarity. Independent claims should clearly specify all essential features needed to define the invention, except insofar as implied by generic terms. The clarity requirement applies to individual claims and the set of claims irrespective of claim type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims producing a product; internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim relates to a process for producing the product of the invention, the process as claimed should be one which, when carried out in a manner reasonable to a PSIA, necessarily results in that particular product; otherwise there is internal inconsistency and lack of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For product claims where invention lies in modifying a well-known product, it suffices that the claim clearly identifies the product and specifies what is modified and how. Similar considerations apply to apparatus claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms likely to cause lack of clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The following terms, when used in claims/descriptions, may be regarded as ambiguous, inadequate, unclear or too broad and lead to lack of clarity: indefinite/relative words (e.g., 'thin', 'wide', 'strong'); terms of approximation (e.g., 'about', 'approximately'); ambiguous adverbs/expressions ('preferably', 'more preferably', 'in particular', 'substantially', 'mostly', 'similarly', 'for example', 'such as'); references ('as described in part ...'); trademarks/trade names/proper names; multiple outcomes (e.g., 'and/or').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More generally, any vague or equivocal wording leaving doubt as to the scope of a feature should be objected to for lack of clarity.
